title: Design an LRU Cache
summary: Everyone knows it is a hash map plus a doubly linked list. The interview is decided by what you do after that: why not a singly linked list, what breaks under concurrency, and what changes when the cache has to survive a restart.

blocks.title: What you are actually being asked
blocks.text: Nobody is testing whether you have memorised *hash map plus doubly linked list*. They are testing whether you can explain **why every other structure fails the O(1) requirement**, and whether you notice that `get` is a write. Get to the answer in ten minutes, then spend the hour on eviction policy, concurrency and persistence.
The problem
Build a fixed-capacity cache with two operations, both in **O(1) average time**:

items: `int get(int key)` — return the value, or `-1` if absent. **A hit counts as a use.**
`void put(int key, int value)` — insert or update. If this pushes the cache over capacity, evict the *least recently used* entry.

blocks.title: The trap is in `get`
blocks.text: `get` mutates the cache. A hit has to move that entry to the front of the recency order, which means `get` takes a write lock, not a read lock. Candidates who model `get` as a pure read write a cache that evicts the hottest key under load.
Clarify before you code

items.title: Is capacity in entries or bytes?
items.text: LeetCode says entries. Real caches are bounded by memory, which turns eviction into *evict until the incoming value fits* — a loop, not a single removal. Ask, then say which one you are building.

items.title: Does an update count as a use?
items.text: `put` on an existing key: does it refresh recency? Almost always yes, and it is a one-line difference. Say it out loud so the interviewer knows you thought about it.

items.title: What happens at capacity zero?
items.text: A cache that cannot hold anything is a legal input and a free correctness point. `put` should be a no-op, not a crash.

items.title: Single-threaded?
items.text: Ask early. The answer changes the data structure, not just the locking — see the concurrency section.

items.title: Do I need eviction callbacks?
items.text: Real caches notify on eviction so callers can flush dirty state. Mention it; do not build it unless asked.

blocks.text: Why the obvious structures fail

blocks.caption: Every one of these is a real answer someone has given. Knowing why they fail is what buys you the trie… sorry, the linked list.
rows: Finding the minimum timestamp is a scan
Not O(1), and updating a key's priority means finding it in the heap
Moving an element to the front is **O(n)** memmove
Unlinking a node needs its **predecessor** — O(n) to find
Nothing fails. This is the answer

blocks.title: Say the singly-linked-list line out loud
blocks.text: *“A singly linked list gets me O(1) at the head but unlinking an arbitrary node needs its predecessor, so I would be scanning. The back pointer is what makes removal O(1).”* That one sentence is the difference between reciting a solution and explaining one.
The structure

blocks.title: Hash map into a doubly linked list
blocks.caption: The map gives O(1) access to the *node*, not the value — that indirection is what makes removal O(1). Sentinel head and tail nodes remove every null check from the pointer surgery.

blocks.title: Class design
blocks.caption: `Node` is deliberately dumb. All invariants live in `LRUCache`, which is the only thing allowed to touch pointers.
blocks.code:
classDiagram
    class LRUCache {
        -int capacity
        -Map~Integer, Node~ map
        -Node head
        -Node tail
        +int get(int key)
        +void put(int key, int value)
        -void addFirst(Node n)
        -void unlink(Node n)
        -Node evictLast()
    }
    class Node {
        +int key
        +int value
        +Node prev
        +Node next
    }
    LRUCache "1" o-- "*" Node : owns

blocks.title: Why `Node` stores its own key
blocks.text: On eviction you have the tail *node* and you need to delete its entry from the map. Without `node.key` you cannot, and you end up with a map full of pointers to unlinked nodes — a leak that passes every test and dies in production.
The code

blocks.title: The library answer is a trap you should spring yourself
blocks.text: Java has `LinkedHashMap` with `accessOrder=true` and `removeEldestEntry`; Python has `OrderedDict`; both are exactly this structure. **Mention it, then build it by hand.** Leading with the library reads as dodging the question; mentioning it after shows you know the ecosystem. If the interviewer says “just use the library”, you have saved twenty minutes for the follow-ups.
Complexity

rows: O(1) — one map lookup, two pointer rewrites
O(capacity) — one node and one map entry per key

blocks.title: “O(1)” is amortised, and you should say so
blocks.text: Hash map operations are O(1) *average*. A resize is O(n), and an adversarial key set degrades lookups. It never matters for the interview, but naming it costs one sentence and separates you from someone reciting a complexity table.
Concurrency — the follow-up that decides it
*“Now make it thread-safe.”* The naive answer is `synchronized` on both methods. The graded answer starts by naming why this is harder than it looks.

items: **Every operation is a write.** `get` relinks nodes, so a read-write lock gives you nothing — all callers take the exclusive lock anyway.
**The list is a single point of contention.** Every hit touches `head`. Throughput is capped by one cache line no matter how many cores you have.
**`ConcurrentHashMap` alone is not enough.** It protects the map; the list pointers are still raced. Two threads unlinking adjacent nodes corrupt the chain.

blocks.caption: What real caches actually do.
rows: The right first answer. Say it, then improve it
**Striped / sharded cache** — N independent LRUs, key hashed to a shard
N× the contention headroom; eviction becomes per-shard
Lock-free reads — a hit just sets a bit
When reads dominate and exactness is negotiable
Reads append to a ring buffer, replayed in batch

blocks.title: The sentence that lands
blocks.text: *“Because `get` mutates recency, a read-write lock buys nothing — so I would shard the cache by key hash and accept that LRU becomes per-shard rather than global. That is the trade real caches make.”* Sharding is the answer they are listening for.
Follow-ups you should have ready

items.title: Make it an LFU cache
items.text: LeetCode 460. Frequency buckets: a map from key to node, plus a map from frequency to a doubly linked list of nodes at that frequency, plus a running `minFreq`. Promotion moves a node between buckets in O(1); eviction takes the tail of the `minFreq` bucket.

items.title: Add TTL per entry
items.text: Store an expiry on the node. Lazy expiry on read is O(1) and leaks memory for keys never read again; a background sweeper reclaims it at the cost of a thread. Most caches do both.

items.title: Make it thread-safe and measure it
items.text: Shard by `key.hashCode()`. Say up front that global LRU becomes approximate — a hot key in one shard can evict entries a global policy would have kept.

items.title: Bound by bytes, not entries
items.text: Eviction becomes a `while` loop, and a single value larger than the whole capacity has to be rejected rather than looped on forever.

items.title: Survive a restart
items.text: This is the pivot to HLD. Write-through to disk for durability, or a warm-up that replays a key log on boot. Redis with `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` is this exact structure with persistence bolted on.

items.title: Distribute it
items.text: Consistent hashing to place keys on nodes, which means eviction is per-node and there is no global recency order at all. Naming that loss is the answer.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state before you are asked

items: `capacity = 0` → every `put` is a no-op, every `get` returns `-1`.
`put` on an existing key updates the value **and** refreshes recency — it must not grow the map.
Evicting when `capacity == 1` — the node being evicted may be the one just inserted if you order the operations wrong. Insert after evicting.
`get` on a key that was evicted returns `-1`, and the map must not still hold it.
Negative and zero values are legal payloads; `-1` is only a sentinel for the *return* of `get`. If values can be `-1`, the contract needs `Integer`/`Optional` instead.

blocks.text: What you are graded on

rows: “Hash map and a doubly linked list”
Explains why singly linked and heap both fail
Notices it is a write, and says so before being asked
Stores the key, and explains the eviction reason
Sentinels, so insert and unlink are unconditional
Mentions it after building, not instead of
Sharding, and names what LRU loses when you shard

blocks.title: The 45-minute plan
blocks.text: **0–5** clarify capacity units and whether `get` refreshes. **5–10** walk the failed structures out loud, land on the doubly linked list. **10–25** code it: sentinels first, then `get`, then `put`, then eviction. **25–32** edge cases and tests. **32–45** concurrency and one of LFU or TTL. If you are still writing pointer code at minute 30, you clarified too little and typed too much.
